fact: System development methodology refers to the structured approaches, models and techniques used to plan, analyse, design, implement and maintain information systems
Developing information systems without a clear methodology often leads to cost overruns, missed deadlines, and systems that fail to meet user and business requirements

Systems Development Methodology is the standard process followed by an organisation to conduct all the steps necessary to analyse, design, implement and maintain information systems; it is a framework used to structure, plan and control the development of an information system
The methodologies covered are Waterfall, Rapid Application Development, Prototyping, the Incremental model and Agile
The Waterfall methodology is a traditional, linear approach in which each phase must be completed before the next begins, proceeding sequentially like a natural waterfall
In Waterfall the key deliverables for each phase are presented to the approval committee and project sponsor for approval before the project moves to the next phase
Strict monitoring in Waterfall is ensured through extensive written documentation, formal reviews, and user and information technology management sign-off at the end of each phase
The Waterfall model has two very important variants: Parallel Development and the V-Model

The four advantages of Waterfall are that it is easy to understand and easy to use; it provides structure to inexperienced staff; the sequential approach and strict controls ensure adequate documentation and design reviews, giving quality, reliability and maintainability; and progress is measurable

The six disadvantages of Waterfall are that it is inflexible, slow, costly and cumbersome; forward-only progress gives a false impression of progress; there is little opportunity for the customer to preview the system until it may be too late; problems are often not discovered until system testing; it is difficult to respond to changes; and it produces excessive documentation that is time-consuming to keep updated

Waterfall is used when the project is a transaction-oriented batch system; is large, expensive and complicated; has clear objectives and a solution; has no pressure for immediate implementation; has clear and comprehensive requirements; has requirements stable during the life cycle; and when the project team is not experienced or may change during implementation
The Waterfall model is best suited for projects with stable and well-understood requirements, such as government systems, financial applications, and regulatory or safety-critical systems

The Parallel Model is a variant of Waterfall designed to reduce the long development time of strictly sequential phases; it keeps the structured predictive nature but allows certain activities to be carried out simultaneously

In the Parallel Model the overall system is divided into subprojects or modules AFTER the general analysis and high-level design phases are completed; each subproject then moves through detailed design, implementation and testing at the same time as the others, and once all are complete they are integrated into a single system

V in the V-Shape Model stands for VERIFICATION and VALIDATION; it is a variant of Waterfall that emphasises testing at each development phase, keeping a sequential structure but establishing a direct relationship between each development phase and its corresponding testing phase

In the V-Shape Model development activities proceed DOWN the left side of the V while testing activities move UP the right side, so verification and validation are built in from the beginning rather than deferred to the end

The five advantages of the V-Shaped Model are that it is simple and straightforward; it improves overall quality through early development of test plans; project management can track progress by milestones; deliverables are high quality because of test effectiveness; and verification and validation are done early in development

The four disadvantages of the V-Shaped Model are that it is affected by the rigidity of the waterfall model; it does not easily handle dynamic changes in requirements; it does not suit the dynamic nature of the business environment; and it does not contain risk analysis activities

The V-Shaped Model is used when systems require high reliability, for example hospital patient control applications; when all requirements are known up front; and when the solution and technology to be used are known

RAD, also called iterative development, uses specialised techniques and computer tools to speed up the analysis, design and implementation phases, enabling a portion of the system to be developed quickly and delivered to users for evaluation and feedback

RAD emphasises quick development and delivery through reusable components, visual development tools and intensive user involvement, aiming to deliver a high-quality system at relatively low investment cost, and reduces project risk by breaking the project into smaller segments

RAD tools include Graphical User Interface builders, Computer-Aided Software Engineering tools, Database Management Systems, fourth-generation programming languages, code generators, and object-oriented techniques

The five RAD advantages are that focus moves from documentation to code, described as WYSIWYG; user feedback makes the model very effective; the time-box approach mitigates cost and schedule risk; cost of development is lower because the system matches user expectations; and important additional requirements may be identified and incorporated into subsequent versions

The five RAD disadvantages are that users begin to work with a system that is intentionally incomplete, which is the chief disadvantage of iterative development; more speed and lower cost may lower overall quality; user expectations may increase and requirements expand, leading to scope creep; there is a risk of never achieving closure; and developers and customers must commit to rapid-fire activities in an abbreviated time frame

RAD is used when requirements are reasonably well known, the user will be involved throughout the life cycle, technical risks are low, high performance is not required, and functionality is delivered in increments

The Incremental model develops the system in small manageable portions called increments, each adding new functionality and building on previous releases; it combines linear and iterative methodologies and sits between waterfall and prototyping

In the Incremental model customers outline the required services, which are prioritised and grouped into increments; the first increment is defined in detail and developed, and later increments are integrated with existing ones; further requirements analysis can still be done for later increments, but changes for the CURRENT increment cannot be accepted

The seven advantages of the Incremental model are developing high-risk or major functions first; each release delivers an operational product; lower initial delivery cost; a divide and conquer breakdown of tasks; faster initial product delivery; customers get important functionality early; and reduced risk of changing requirements and overall project failure

The five disadvantages of the Incremental model are difficulty mapping customer requirements to increments of the right size; difficulty identifying common facilities needed by all requirements; the need for good planning and design; the need for early definition of a complete and fully functional system so increments can be defined; and the need for well-defined module interfaces

Prototyping builds prototypes early to enable early feedback and analysis; a quick and dirty version with minimal features is built, then reanalysed, redesigned and reimplemented after user reactions, and the cycle continues until analysts, users and sponsor agree the prototype has enough functionality to be installed
There are two types of prototyping: THROWAWAY prototyping and EVOLUTIONARY prototyping

Evolutionary prototyping builds an initial version and gradually refines and expands it until it becomes the final operational system, evolving through continuous user feedback and iterative enhancements; its objective is to deliver a working system to end users, and development starts with the requirements that are best understood

In evolutionary prototyping the designer builds the database, the user interface and the algorithmic functions, then demonstrates the prototype, and the user evaluates for problems and suggests improvements; this loop continues until the user is satisfied and the prototype becomes the final system

The advantages of evolutionary prototyping are that customers can SEE requirements as they are gathered; a more accurate product is developed; unexpected requirements can be accommodated; developers learn from customers; design and development stay flexible; and interaction with the prototype stimulates awareness of additional needed functionality

The disadvantages of evolutionary prototyping are a tendency to abandon structured program development for code-and-fix; lack of careful methodical analysis before design and implementation decisions; a bad reputation for quick-and-dirty methods; overall maintainability may be overlooked; the customer may want the prototype delivered; and the process may continue forever, which is scope creep

Evolutionary prototyping is used when requirements are unstable or need clarification, as the requirements clarification stage of a waterfall model, to develop user interfaces, for short-lived demonstrations, for new original development, and with the analysis and design portions of object-oriented development

Throwaway prototyping, also called rapid or exploratory prototyping, creates a temporary prototype to help users and analysts understand requirements; prototypes explore design alternatives rather than the actual new system, are built quickly and DISCARDED after requirements are clarified, and the actual system is then developed using a more structured methodology

Throwaway prototyping has a thorough analysis phase to gather requirements first; design prototypes are then developed to understand issues that are not fully understood or carry technical risk, which reduces risk and produces more stable, reliable systems

Throwaway prototyping is used when requirements are unclear or users cannot articulate needs easily; evolutionary prototyping is used when requirements evolve and rapid delivery is required, and it risks weak architecture and difficult documentation

The Agile model is a group of software development methods based on adaptive, iterative and incremental development in which every iteration is a complete software project; modelling and documentation overhead is eliminated while face-to-face communication is preferred

In Agile, development is carried out in short time-boxed cycles known as iterations or sprints; each sprint typically includes requirement analysis, design, coding, testing and review, and at the end of each sprint a working increment is delivered for user evaluation and feedback

Agile activities are creation and prioritisation of user stories or requirements, sprint planning and task assignment, development and testing within each sprint, and sprint review and retrospective for feedback and improvement
Popular agile methods are Crystal Clear, Scrum, Extreme Programming, Lean Software Development, and Kanban
The first challenge for project managers is selecting the methodology, and choosing is not simple because no one methodology is always best
The six methodology selection criteria are clarity of user requirements, familiarity with technology, system complexity, system reliability, short time schedules, and schedule visibility
Clarity of user requirements: when requirements are unclear, system prototyping and throwaway prototyping are more appropriate, because they give users prototypes to interact with early in the SDLC

Familiarity with technology: throwaway prototyping is particularly appropriate where there is a lack of familiarity with the technology, because it explicitly encourages developers to create design prototypes for areas with high risk
System complexity: complex systems require careful and detailed analysis and design, and throwaway prototyping is well suited to that, but system prototyping is NOT

System reliability: the V-model is useful when reliability is important because it emphasises testing, and throwaway prototyping is most appropriate when reliability is a high priority because detailed analysis and design are combined with the ability to test many approaches through design prototypes; examples of critical reliability are medical equipment and missile control systems, against merely important cases such as games and internet video

Short time schedules: projects with short schedules suit RAD methodologies because they are designed to accelerate development, and iterative development and system prototyping are excellent choices because the team can adjust system functionality to meet a specific delivery date
Schedule visibility: RAD methodologies move many critical design decisions earlier in the project so managers can recognise and address risk factors and keep expectations in check

No single methodology suits all projects; traditional methodologies are effective for well-defined stable projects, while adaptive approaches such as Agile and prototyping suit dynamic environments with evolving requirements
